violations.title: Line height below what the writing system needs
violations.selector: #root > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > form > div:nth-of-type(2)
violations.snippet: عند قيامكم بالتسجيل، فهذا يعني موافقتكم على
violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.14 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.title: Physical text alignment in a right-to-left context
violations.selector: #news-feed-container > section:nth-of-type(2) > footer > a
violations.snippet: المزيد
violations.whatIsWrong: This element holds Arabic text in a right-to-left context and sets text-align: left.
violations.whyItMatters: text-align: left pushes this text to the far side of its own line, against the direction it reads in. Physical values address the screen rather than the reader, so they do not flip when the direction does, and here the side named is the wrong side already.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.selector: #news-feed-container > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h3 > a > span
violations.snippet: 5 جبهات وباب المندب.. كيف اتسع التصعيد العسكري في اليمن؟
violations.whatIsWrong: hyphens: auto is applied to Arabic text.
violations.whyItMatters: Automatic hyphenation cuts a word in two and inserts a hyphen. Arabic has no hyphenation convention, and the cut falls between joined letters, so the word is severed and a mark that means nothing in this script is added at the seam.
violations.howToFix: Set hyphens: manual for Arabic text, and scope hyphens: auto to the languages that have a hyphenation dictionary.

violations.whatIsWrong: hyphens: auto is applied to Arabic text.
violations.whyItMatters: Automatic hyphenation cuts a word in two and inserts a hyphen. Arabic has no hyphenation convention, and the cut falls between joined letters, so the word is severed and a mark that means nothing in this script is added at the seam.
violations.howToFix: Set hyphens: manual for Arabic text, and scope hyphens: auto to the languages that have a hyphenation dictionary.

violations.title: Case transform applied to a script without case
violations.selector: #featured-news-container > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h2
violations.snippet: اختيارات المحررين
violations.whatIsWrong: text-transform: uppercase is applied to Arabic text.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic has no upper and lower case, so there is nothing for the browser to convert and the declaration does nothing at all. What it does tell you is that this CSS was designed around Latin and reached the translation unread — and a stylesheet in that state usually carries assumptions that are not harmless, about direction, spacing or line height.
violations.howToFix: Remove text-transform from this text, or scope the declaration to the languages that have case with :lang(). Then read the rest of the same block for the assumptions that travelled with it.

violations.title: Declared font stack does not appear to cover the script
violations.selector: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
violations.snippet: الحدث
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is set in alarabiya, Helvetica Neue, sans-serif, and measurement during the scan suggests none of those families is the one rendering it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page is leaving Arabic to whatever font the system of the reader happens to substitute. That font was not chosen for this script and may shape it poorly, size it inconsistently against the Latin beside it, or fail to draw parts of it at all. The result is a page that looks unfinished in one language and finished in every other.
violations.howToFix: Add a font that covers Arabic to the stack for this text, and make sure it is actually served — a family named in CSS but never loaded behaves exactly like a family that was never named. Check it in a browser on a machine where that font is not installed, which is the situation most readers are in.

violations.whyItMatters: The page is leaving Arabic to whatever font the system of the reader happens to substitute. That font was not chosen for this script and may shape it poorly, size it inconsistently against the Latin beside it, or fail to draw parts of it at all. The result is a page that looks unfinished in one language and finished in every other.
violations.howToFix: Add a font that covers Arabic to the stack for this text, and make sure it is actually served — a family named in CSS but never loaded behaves exactly like a family that was never named. Check it in a browser on a machine where that font is not installed, which is the situation most readers are in.

violations.selector: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > section:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h2
violations.snippet: زيلينسكي: روسيا استخدمت صواريخ بالستية كورية شمالية في قصف أ…
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text carrying stacked marks is cut off by a container 75px tall: the content needs 78px and the box hides everything past 75px.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks stacked above the letter, or parts that hang below it. A container sized against Latin cuts that ink off, and the loss is not cosmetic: the mark is what distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another. A clipped Latin word is still that word, shortened. A clipped tone mark is a different word.
violations.howToFix: Let the container grow with its content, or give it enough height for the text it holds. Where truncation is deliberate, fade or ellipsis the text rather than cutting it with overflow: hidden, so the reader can tell that something is missing.

violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.14 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.selector: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(9) > a
violations.snippet: منوعات
violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.13 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.snippet: أميركا
violations.whatIsWrong: This element holds Arabic text in a right-to-left context and sets text-align: right.
violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.title: Unisolated left-to-right run inside right-to-left text
violations.selector: #panel-1 > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a > span:nth-of-type(2)
violations.snippet: العيون إلى السماء.. 4 ظواهر فلكية متزامنة في يوم واحد
violations.whatIsWrong: The run ".. 4" is embedded in Arabic text next to punctuation, and nothing isolates it from the text around it.
violations.whyItMatters: Punctuation has no direction of its own, so the bidirectional algorithm gives it the direction of whatever sits beside it. Around an embedded left-to-right run that decision can put a full stop, a bracket or a quotation mark at the opposite end of the clause from where it was written. The words are all present and the sentence reads wrongly, which is harder to spot and harder to report than text that is simply missing.
violations.howToFix: Wrap the embedded run in <bdi>, which isolates it and is what the element exists for. Where markup cannot be added, the Unicode isolate characters U+2068 and U+2069 around the run do the same job. Isolation on the paragraph does not help: it has to wrap the run itself.

violations.title: Case transform applied to a script without case
violations.selector: html > body > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > span:nth-of-type(1) > b
violations.snippet: عاجل
violations.whatIsWrong: text-transform: uppercase is applied to Arabic text.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic has no upper and lower case, so there is nothing for the browser to convert and the declaration does nothing at all. What it does tell you is that this CSS was designed around Latin and reached the translation unread — and a stylesheet in that state usually carries assumptions that are not harmless, about direction, spacing or line height.
violations.howToFix: Remove text-transform from this text, or scope the declaration to the languages that have case with :lang(). Then read the rest of the same block for the assumptions that travelled with it.

violations.title: Directional icon not mirrored in a right-to-left context
violations.selector: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > section:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(4) > a
violations.snippet: كيف واجهت دول آسيان «صدمة هرمز»؟
violations.whatIsWrong: This element sits in a right-to-left context and names a horizontal direction via the character «, with no transform on it or on any ancestor that reverses or turns it.
violations.whyItMatters: Forward runs leftward for a Arabic reader, so an arrow taken from the left-to-right design points back the way they came. Nothing about it looks broken — it looks like a control that goes the other way, which is why this survives review and reaches the reader as a navigation that argues with itself.
violations.howToFix: Mirror the icon in the right-to-left context, with a [dir="rtl"] selector applying transform: scaleX(-1), or by swapping in the mirrored glyph. Leave alone the arrows that point at something other than the reading direction, such as a media play control.

violations.title: Right-to-left text with no direction declared
violations.selector: #Cheif
violations.snippet: محمد إبراهيم الدسوقي
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text has no dir attribute on it or on any element above it, and is being laid out left-to-right.
violations.whyItMatters: Without a base direction the paragraph is treated as left-to-right, so Arabic words are placed correctly but everything around them is not. Punctuation ends up on the wrong side, brackets and quotation marks reverse, and any number or Latin word in the line is ordered against the reader. The text is present and the sentence is wrong.
violations.howToFix: Add dir="rtl" to the element that holds this text, or to the nearest block that contains it — on <html> when the whole page is in this language. Where the direction depends on content written by users, dir="auto" is the correct answer and this rule accepts it.

violations.title: Declared font stack does not appear to cover the script
violations.selector: #Cheif
violations.snippet: محمد إبراهيم الدسوقي
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is set in Conv_GE SS Two Medium, and measurement during the scan suggests none of those families is the one rendering it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page is leaving Arabic to whatever font the system of the reader happens to substitute. That font was not chosen for this script and may shape it poorly, size it inconsistently against the Latin beside it, or fail to draw parts of it at all. The result is a page that looks unfinished in one language and finished in every other.
violations.howToFix: Add a font that covers Arabic to the stack for this text, and make sure it is actually served — a family named in CSS but never loaded behaves exactly like a family that was never named. Check it in a browser on a machine where that font is not installed, which is the situation most readers are in.

violations.snippet: بقلم: محمد إبراهيم الدسوقي
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is set in Conv_GE SS Two Medium, and measurement during the scan suggests none of those families is the one rendering it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page is leaving Arabic to whatever font the system of the reader happens to substitute. That font was not chosen for this script and may shape it poorly, size it inconsistently against the Latin beside it, or fail to draw parts of it at all. The result is a page that looks unfinished in one language and finished in every other.
violations.howToFix: Add a font that covers Arabic to the stack for this text, and make sure it is actually served — a family named in CSS but never loaded behaves exactly like a family that was never named. Check it in a browser on a machine where that font is not installed, which is the situation most readers are in.

violations.title: Line height below what the writing system needs
violations.selector: #cars > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > h4
violations.snippet: المزيد +
violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.2 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.2 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.whyItMatters: The page looks right, so this is easy to leave alone. CSS direction settles the visual layout and stops there: the dir attribute is what travels into the accessibility tree, and it is what a screen reader and a translation tool consult to decide the base direction of the text they are handed. A stylesheet that fails to load takes the direction with it; an attribute does not.
violations.howToFix: Add dir="rtl" to the element that holds this text, or to the nearest block that contains it — on <html> when the whole page is in this language. Where the direction depends on content written by users, dir="auto" is the correct answer and this rule accepts it.

violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is laid out right-to-left by CSS, but no dir attribute is set on it or on any element above it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page looks right, so this is easy to leave alone. CSS direction settles the visual layout and stops there: the dir attribute is what travels into the accessibility tree, and it is what a screen reader and a translation tool consult to decide the base direction of the text they are handed. A stylesheet that fails to load takes the direction with it; an attribute does not.
violations.howToFix: Add dir="rtl" to the element that holds this text, or to the nearest block that contains it — on <html> when the whole page is in this language. Where the direction depends on content written by users, dir="auto" is the correct answer and this rule accepts it.

violations.title: Physical text alignment in a right-to-left context
violations.selector: #Li1 > a
violations.snippet: EN
violations.whatIsWrong: This element holds Latin text in a right-to-left context and sets text-align: right.
violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.title: Unisolated left-to-right run inside right-to-left text
violations.selector: #sm-text > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a > h3
violations.snippet: الصيدلة 80% والهندسة 78%.. الجامعة المصرية اليابانية تحدد ال…
violations.whatIsWrong: The run "78%.." is embedded in Arabic text next to punctuation, and nothing isolates it from the text around it.
violations.whyItMatters: Punctuation has no direction of its own, so the bidirectional algorithm gives it the direction of whatever sits beside it. Around an embedded left-to-right run that decision can put a full stop, a bracket or a quotation mark at the opposite end of the clause from where it was written. The words are all present and the sentence reads wrongly, which is harder to spot and harder to report than text that is simply missing.
violations.howToFix: Wrap the embedded run in <bdi>, which isolates it and is what the element exists for. Where markup cannot be added, the Unicode isolate characters U+2068 and U+2069 around the run do the same job. Isolation on the paragraph does not help: it has to wrap the run itself.

violations.title: Directional icon not mirrored in a right-to-left context
violations.selector: #cars > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > a > h3
violations.snippet: كأنها خرجت من فيلم قديم.. «جوهرة بريطانية» نادرة تظهر في مصر…
violations.whatIsWrong: This element sits in a right-to-left context and names a horizontal direction via the character «, with no transform on it or on any ancestor that reverses or turns it.
violations.whyItMatters: Forward runs leftward for a Arabic reader, so an arrow taken from the left-to-right design points back the way they came. Nothing about it looks broken — it looks like a control that goes the other way, which is why this survives review and reaches the reader as a navigation that argues with itself.
violations.howToFix: Mirror the icon in the right-to-left context, with a [dir="rtl"] selector applying transform: scaleX(-1), or by swapping in the mirrored glyph. Leave alone the arrows that point at something other than the reading direction, such as a media play control.

violations.title: Text with stacked marks cut off by its container
violations.selector: html > body > main > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(14) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h3 > a
violations.snippet: كارثة زلزال كولومبيا.. 5000 منزل و42 مبنى و3 مستشفيات تحت ال…
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text carrying stacked marks is cut off by a container 65px tall: the content needs 84px and the box hides everything past 65px.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks stacked above the letter, or parts that hang below it. violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.title: Unisolated left-to-right run inside right-to-left text
violations.selector: #news4 > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3 > a
violations.snippet: في تطور مثير للقلق، لم يكن زلزال كولومبيا المدمر الذى ضرب بق…
violations.whatIsWrong: The run "7.4" is embedded in Arabic text next to punctuation, and nothing isolates it from the text around it.
violations.whyItMatters: Punctuation has no direction of its own, so the bidirectional algorithm gives it the direction of whatever sits beside it. Around an embedded left-to-right run that decision can put a full stop, a bracket or a quotation mark at the opposite end of the clause from where it was written. The words are all present and the sentence reads wrongly, which is harder to spot and harder to report than text that is simply missing.
violations.howToFix: Wrap the embedded run in <bdi>, which isolates it and is what the element exists for. Where markup cannot be added, the Unicode isolate characters U+2068 and U+2069 around the run do the same job. Isolation on the paragraph does not help: it has to wrap the run itself.

violations.whatIsWrong: This element sits in a right-to-left context and names a horizontal direction via the character «, with no transform on it or on any ancestor that reverses or turns it.
violations.whyItMatters: Forward runs leftward for a Arabic reader, so an arrow taken from the left-to-right design points back the way they came. violations.howToFix: Mirror the icon in the right-to-left context, with a [dir="rtl"] selector applying transform: scaleX(-1), or by swapping in the mirrored glyph. Leave alone the arrows that point at something other than the reading direction, such as a media play control.

violations.title: Declared font stack does not appear to cover the script
violations.selector: html > body > h1
violations.snippet: أخبار اليوم | سكاي نيوز عربية
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is set in HelveticaNeueReg, and measurement during the scan suggests none of those families is the one rendering it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page is leaving Arabic to whatever font the system of the reader happens to substitute. That font was not chosen for this script and may shape it poorly, size it inconsistently against the Latin beside it, or fail to draw parts of it at all. The result is a page that looks unfinished in one language and finished in every other.
violations.howToFix: Add a font that covers Arabic to the stack for this text, and make sure it is actually served — a family named in CSS but never loaded behaves exactly like a family that was never named. Check it in a browser on a machine where that font is not installed, which is the situation most readers are in.

violations.title: Text with stacked marks cut off by its container
violations.selector: #site-menu > div > nav > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(3) > a
violations.snippet: عاجل
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text carrying stacked marks is cut off by a container 39px tall: the content needs 41px and the box hides everything past 39px.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks stacked above the letter, or parts that hang below it. A container sized against Latin cuts that ink off, and the loss is not cosmetic: the mark is what distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another. A clipped Latin word is still that word, shortened. A clipped tone mark is a different word.
violations.howToFix: Let the container grow with its content, or give it enough height for the text it holds. Where truncation is deliberate, fade or ellipsis the text rather than cutting it with overflow: hidden, so the reader can tell that something is missing.

violations.title: Line height below what the writing system needs
violations.selector: html > body > section > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > a > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > h3

violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.4 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.title: Physical text alignment in a right-to-left context
violations.selector: #site-header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
violations.snippet: الثلاثاء 11 أغسطس 2026
violations.whatIsWrong: This element holds Arabic text in a right-to-left context and sets text-align: right.
violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.title: Unisolated left-to-right run inside right-to-left text
violations.selector: html > body > section > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > a > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > h3
violations.snippet: هونغ كونغ: 72% من المهنيين يستخدمون الذكاء الاصطناعي بانتظام
violations.whatIsWrong: The run ": 72%" is embedded in Arabic text next to punctuation, and nothing isolates it from the text around it.
violations.whyItMatters: Punctuation has no direction of its own, so the bidirectional algorithm gives it the direction of whatever sits beside it. Around an embedded left-to-right run that decision can put a full stop, a bracket or a quotation mark at the opposite end of the clause from where it was written. The words are all present and the sentence reads wrongly, which is harder to spot and harder to report than text that is simply missing.
violations.howToFix: Wrap the embedded run in <bdi>, which isolates it and is what the element exists for. Where markup cannot be added, the Unicode isolate characters U+2068 and U+2069 around the run do the same job. Isolation on the paragraph does not help: it has to wrap the run itself.

Handed Arabic text under this language, it applies the wrong phoneme set — the output is not accented, it is unintelligible, and a listener cannot correct for it the way a sighted reader can skim past a wrong font. Translation tools and hyphenation read the same attribute and get the same wrong answer.
violations.howToFix: Set lang on this element, or on the nearest block containing it, to the language this text is actually written in. violations.title: Right-to-left text with no direction declared
violations.selector: #aswift_1_host > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > span:nth-of-type(1)
violations.snippet: اخبار کی سبسکرپشن
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text has no dir attribute on it or on any element above it, and is being laid out left-to-right.
violations.whyItMatters: Without a base direction the paragraph is treated as left-to-right, so Arabic words are placed correctly but everything around them is not. Punctuation ends up on the wrong side, brackets and quotation marks reverse, and any number or Latin word in the line is ordered against the reader. The text is present and the sentence is wrong.
violations.howToFix: Add dir="rtl" to the element that holds this text, or to the nearest block that contains it — on <html> when the whole page is in this language. Where the direction depends on content written by users, dir="auto" is the correct answer and this rule accepts it.

violations.title: Line height below what the writing system needs
violations.selector: #main-section > section > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(17) > a > p

violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.1 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.whatIsWrong: Line height is 1.2 times the font size on Arabic text, below the 1.5 this script needs. 1.5 is the line spacing named by WCAG SC 1.4.8 (Level AAA).
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

violations.title: Right-to-left text with no direction declared
violations.selector: #main-section > section > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a > h2
violations.snippet: امریکا نے ایران سے مذاکرات شروع کرنے کیلئے بھیک مانگی، عباس …
violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is laid out right-to-left by CSS, but no dir attribute is set on it or on any element above it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page looks right, so this is easy to leave alone. CSS direction settles the visual layout and stops there: the dir attribute is what travels into the accessibility tree, and it is what a screen reader and a translation tool consult to decide the base direction of the text they are handed. A stylesheet that fails to load takes the direction with it; an attribute does not.
violations.howToFix: Add dir="rtl" to the element that holds this text, or to the nearest block that contains it — on <html> when the whole page is in this language. Where the direction depends on content written by users, dir="auto" is the correct answer and this rule accepts it.

violations.whatIsWrong: Arabic text is laid out right-to-left by CSS, but no dir attribute is set on it or on any element above it.
violations.whyItMatters: The page looks right, so this is easy to leave alone. CSS direction settles the visual layout and stops there: the dir attribute is what travels into the accessibility tree, and it is what a screen reader and a translation tool consult to decide the base direction of the text they are handed. A stylesheet that fails to load takes the direction with it; an attribute does not.
violations.howToFix: Add dir="rtl" to the element that holds this text, or to the nearest block that contains it — on <html> when the whole page is in this language. Where the direction depends on content written by users, dir="auto" is the correct answer and this rule accepts it.

violations.whyItMatters: The page looks right, so this is easy to leave alone. CSS direction settles the visual layout and stops there: the dir attribute is what travels into the accessibility tree, and it is what a screen reader and a translation tool consult to decide the base direction of the text they are handed. A stylesheet that fails to load takes the direction with it; an attribute does not.

violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.whatIsWrong: This element holds Arabic text in a right-to-left context and sets text-align: right.
violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.title: Unisolated left-to-right run inside right-to-left text
violations.selector: #main-section > section > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > h1
violations.snippet: آئی ایم ایف سے 1.2 ارب ڈالر ملنے کا امکان، حکومت نے تیاری شر…
violations.whatIsWrong: The run "1.2" is embedded in Arabic text next to punctuation, and nothing isolates it from the text around it.
violations.whyItMatters: Punctuation has no direction of its own, so the bidirectional algorithm gives it the direction of whatever sits beside it. Around an embedded left-to-right run that decision can put a full stop, a bracket or a quotation mark at the opposite end of the clause from where it was written. The words are all present and the sentence reads wrongly, which is harder to spot and harder to report than text that is simply missing.
violations.howToFix: Wrap the embedded run in <bdi>, which isolates it and is what the element exists for. Where markup cannot be added, the Unicode isolate characters U+2068 and U+2069 around the run do the same job. Isolation on the paragraph does not help: it has to wrap the run itself.

violations.title: Case transform applied to a script without case
violations.selector: #link-3 > a
violations.snippet: مزید
violations.whatIsWrong: text-transform: uppercase is applied to Arabic text.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic has no upper and lower case, so there is nothing for the browser to convert and the declaration does nothing at all. What it does tell you is that this CSS was designed around Latin and reached the translation unread — and a stylesheet in that state usually carries assumptions that are not harmless, about direction, spacing or line height.
violations.howToFix: Remove text-transform from this text, or scope the declaration to the languages that have case with :lang(). Then read the rest of the same block for the assumptions that travelled with it.

What it does tell you is that this CSS was designed around Latin and reached the translation unread — and a stylesheet in that state usually carries assumptions that are not harmless, about direction, spacing or line height.
violations.howToFix: Remove text-transform from this text, or scope the declaration to the languages that have case with :lang(). Then read the rest of the same block for the assumptions that travelled with it.

violations.title: Letter spacing applied to a cursive script
violations.selector: #text-blink
violations.snippet: لائیو
violations.whatIsWrong: letter-spacing is set to 1px on Arabic text.
violations.whyItMatters: Arabic is a cursive script: its letters connect, and the connection is part of how a word is read. Tracking pulls the letters apart at exactly the points where they should join, so the word arrives as a row of disconnected shapes; negative tracking collides them instead. A reader does not see loose text, they see text that has come apart.
violations.howToFix: Remove letter-spacing from this element, or scope it so it reaches Latin runs only — for example :lang(en) or a selector that excludes [dir="rtl"] — rather than applying it to every language the page is translated into.

violations.title: Declared language does not match the script of the text
violations.selector: html > body > section:nth-of-type(8) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > ul > div > li:nth-of-type(10) > a
violations.snippet: Science & Technology News
violations.whatIsWrong: The nearest declared language is lang="ur", which is written in Arabic, but 100% of this text is Latin.
violations.whyItMatters: A screen reader chooses its voice and its pronunciation rules from the declared language. Handed Latin text under this language, it applies the wrong phoneme set — the output is not accented, it is unintelligible, and a listener cannot correct for it the way a sighted reader can skim past a wrong font. Translation tools and hyphenation read the same attribute and get the same wrong answer.
violations.howToFix: Set lang on this element, or on the nearest block containing it, to the language this text is actually written in. If the language is right and the script is the unusual one, say so explicitly with a BCP-47 script subtag — sr-Latn, zh-Hans, ku-Arab — which this rule accepts as final.

violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks stacked above the letter, or parts that hang below it. A container sized against Latin cuts that ink off, and the loss is not cosmetic: the mark is what distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another. A clipped Latin word is still that word, shortened. A clipped tone mark is a different word.
violations.howToFix: Raise the line clamp, or give the box room for the marks by increasing its line-height so each clamped line carries its full ink. If the truncation is deliberate, check what the last visible line actually reads as in this script.

violations.whyItMatters: Arabic places ink outside the box that Latin fits inside — marks that stack above the letter, or parts that hang below it. Leading chosen for Latin leaves that ink nowhere to go, so it touches or overlaps the line above. What collides is not decoration: it is the mark that distinguishes one letter, or one tone, from another.
violations.howToFix: Raise line-height to at least 1.5 for this text, or remove the declaration and let line-height: normal use the metrics the font ships with. If the value is deliberate for Latin, scope it with :lang() rather than applying it to every translation of the page.

CSS direction settles the visual layout and stops there: the dir attribute is what travels into the accessibility tree, and it is what a screen reader and a translation tool consult to decide the base direction of the text they are handed. violations.snippet: متعلقہ خبریں
violations.whatIsWrong: This element holds Arabic text in a right-to-left context and sets text-align: right.
violations.whyItMatters: text-align: right happens to look correct here, which is what makes it worth reporting: it names a side of the screen rather than an end of the line, so it stops looking correct the moment this component is rendered left-to-right. The version of the page nobody tested is the one where it shows.
violations.howToFix: Use the logical values instead: text-align: start for the side the line begins on, text-align: end for the side it finishes on. They resolve against the direction of the text, so one declaration serves both directions and there is nothing left to mirror by hand.

violations.title: Unisolated left-to-right run inside right-to-left text
violations.selector: html > body > section:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > ul:nth-of-type(2) > li:nth-of-type(6) > a > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3
violations.snippet: اسلام آباد ہائیکورٹ: 3 نئے ایڈیشنل ججز نے حلف اٹھا لیا
violations.whatIsWrong: The run ": 3" is embedded in Arabic text next to punctuation, and nothing isolates it from the text around it.
violations.whyItMatters: Punctuation has no direction of its own, so the bidirectional algorithm gives it the direction of whatever sits beside it. Around an embedded left-to-right run that decision can put a full stop, a bracket or a quotation mark at the opposite end of the clause from where it was written. The words are all present and the sentence reads wrongly, which is harder to spot and harder to report than text that is simply missing.
violations.howToFix: Wrap the embedded run in <bdi>, which isolates it and is what the element exists for. Where markup cannot be added, the Unicode isolate characters U+2068 and U+2069 around the run do the same job. Isolation on the paragraph does not help: it has to wrap the run itself.

standard.title: All page content should be contained by landmarks
Links must have discernible text
Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds
Alternative text of images should not be repeated as text
Heading levels should only increase by one
Headings should not be empty
<ul> and <ol> must only directly contain <li>, <script> or <template> elements
<li> elements must be contained in a <ul> or <ol>
Images must have alternative text
ARIA role should be appropriate for the element
Form elements must have labels
Frames must have an accessible name
Document should have one main landmark
Inline text spacing must be adjustable with custom stylesheets
Elements marked as presentational should be consistently ignored
Buttons must have discernible text
Interactive controls must not be nested
Documents must have <title> element to aid in navigation
Main landmark should not be contained in another landmark
Landmarks should have a unique role or role/label/title (i.e. accessible name) combination
<marquee> elements are deprecated and must not be used

Declared font stack does not appear to cover the script
Case transform applied to a script without case
Directional icon not mirrored in a right-to-left context
